newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Kiev says Denver G7 summit crucial for Chernobyl.
newsitem.headline: Kiev says Denver G7 summit crucial for Chernobyl.

text.p: Ukraine, years into talks on financing the closure of the Chernobyl nuclear power station, is looking to this week's Denver summit of the Group of Seven rich industrial nations in the hope of concrete financial solutions.

Kiev's hopes for the G7 are focused on two issues -- a $780 million grant for the stricken plant's fourth reactor and its "sarcophagus" covering and money to build two new reactors to replace electricity to be lost by Chernobyl's closure in 2000.
"The G7 should find ways of financing the sarcophagus and problems associated with it," top Chernobyl negotiator and Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko told Reuters on Thursday.
"Denver's decisions are going to be crucial. We hope the final communique will mention the G7 obligation to finance the project dealing with the tomb (sarcophagus)," he added.

The plan to deal with the ruined reactor, containing a nearly 200-tonne nuclear fuel and concrete mixture, is to stabilise the shell hurriedly built by thousands of workers after the devastating explosion of April 1986.
It includes removing fuel with special equipment.
Kostenko said the $780 million, to be delivered as a grant, would be spent over seven years.

In a further development, Kostenko said an international conference would be held in September in London or Washington. It would be chaired by Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma, U.S. Vice-President Al Gore and European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) president Jacques de Larosiere.
"This conference will decide how much in particular everyone is due to spend on the fourth reactor, after Denver sets the total amount," Kostenko said.

Volodymyr Horbulin, secretary of the policy-making Security and Defence Council, said on Wednesday that Kiev's leadership recently received letters from Gore and President Bill Clinton, which "showed the decisiveness of the U.S. administration and a new aproach towards Chernobyl".

Horbulin said: "The Denver summit has the intention of finding a solution on how to finance Chernobyl -- not from the point of view of energy but from a safety standpoint, because it is a dangerous site."
The explosion of the fourth reactor 11 years ago sent a radiation cloud over Russia, Belarus and much of Europe.

Another issue to be discussed in Denver is the completion of two nuclear reactors at the Rivne and Khmelnitsky plants in western Ukraine. The EBRD is due to decide at the end of this month whether to go ahead with a $1.2 billion credit.
"We expect reassurances of a commitment by G7 nations to provide financing for completion. We expect this subject to be included in the communique," Kostenko said.

"To be able to physically stop all Chernobyl's reactors by 2000 depends on when this money would come through," Kostenko said. "We cannot allow gaps in the supply of electricity and there must be compensation for loss of Chernobyl's power."
Chernobyl produces five percent of Ukraine's electricity while another five nuclear plants produce 45 percent.

"The completion of Rivne-4 and Khmelnitsky-2 is not only Ukraine's wish but also the G7's commitment which was taken earlier," Kostenko said, referring to last year's memoranduum of understanding signed in Canada between Ukraine and G7.
